issue: Can a change in § 924(c)'s anti-stacking rule, which the First Step Act made prospective only, be an extraordinary and compelling reason for compassionate release, including through U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)?

sides.position: The § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment cannot be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction, because that would give the prospective-only amendment retroactive effect that Congress withheld. This includes rejecting § 1B1.13(b)(6) as applied to this change.
cases: United States v. Thacker, 4 F.4th 569 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Austin, 125 F.4th 688 (5th Cir. 2025)
United States v. McCall, 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1185 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
United States v. Black, No. 24-1191 (7th Cir. 2025)

sides.position: The § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment can be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction, including through the Commission's policy statement in § 1B1.13(b)(6).
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, 26 F.4th 14 (1st Cir. 2022)
United States v. McCoy, 981 F.3d 271 (4th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Chen, 48 F.4th 1092 (9th Cir. 2022)
United States v. McGee, 992 F.3d 1035 (10th Cir. 2021)

this_court: Follows Thacker and joins the Third Circuit, holding that the § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment cannot be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction, notwithstanding § 1B1.13(b)(6). The opinion says the Supreme Court may still resolve the split.
quote: We recognize Thacker's holding that § 924(c)'s anti-stacking amendment cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction is not consensus; the courts of appeals have split on the issue.
cite: United States v. Eural Black, No. 24-1191 (7th Cir. 2025)
